summary: Swiggy helps people order restaurant meals, receive groceries through Instamart, and use dining or event services. The group also provides storage and distribution services to businesses.
description: A customer choosing dinner needs a restaurant to cook and a delivery worker to bring it. A customer ordering groceries needs stocked goods, picking and delivery. Swiggy arranges these different jobs through its services; an app order still requires people and physical work behind the screen.
money: The group earns under each service’s terms, including fees for arranging orders, delivery-related charges, advertising, memberships and goods or distribution sales. It pays for workers and partners, storage sites, technology and promotions. It does not keep every amount collected from customers.
customers: People order meals, groceries and experiences. Restaurants and sellers use services to reach buyers. Businesses also pay for storage, distribution or related services that move goods through the buying and selling chain.
drivers: Repeat orders, the amount bought, charges earned, the cost of picking and delivery, nearby demand, discounts and the money needed to open and support new services.

groups.title: Restaurant food delivery
groups.examples: Finding a restaurant, placing an order and receiving the meal.
groups.explanation: The restaurant prepares the food. Swiggy helps arrange the order, payment and delivery. The restaurant and other providers receive their agreed amounts, so the meal’s full price is not all Swiggy income.

groups.title: Instamart grocery shopping
groups.examples: Groceries and household goods delivered from nearby sites.
groups.explanation: A dark store is a place where workers store, pick and pack goods for online orders rather than serve shoppers in aisles. A grocery order needs the right stock, packing and a delivery route; the merchant and stock arrangements determine who earns which part of the payment.

groups.title: Dining and experiences
groups.explanation: These services help customers arrange dining or events away from home. Reservations, payments and venue arrangements are different from picking and delivering groceries.

groups.title: Storage, distribution and newer services
groups.examples: Services for merchants and brands, plus newer offerings being developed.
groups.explanation: Distribution means getting goods from suppliers towards the businesses that sell or use them. Storage and movement can create a large goods-sales total but also involve buying goods, running warehouses and transporting them. A new app feature is not automatically a separate profitable business.

basics.title: The checkout total is not the amount Swiggy keeps
basics.text: Order value measures customer transactions on the company’s stated basis. Revenue is the income recorded by the company under its own arrangements. Money owed to restaurants and sellers is not automatically its profit.

basics.title: Covering an order’s direct costs is only a first step
basics.text: A headline measure may compare income with a selected set of delivery and order costs. Offices, technology, financing and other expenses can remain outside it. Check what costs are included before accepting a claim of breakeven, meaning costs have been covered.

steps.title: The customer chooses what they need
steps.text: Select a meal, goods or an experience through the relevant service.

steps.title: Confirm who will supply it
steps.text: Pass the meal request to a restaurant, locate merchant stock or confirm the venue arrangement.

steps.title: Complete the order
steps.text: Have the food prepared, pick and pack groceries, arrange delivery or complete the dining transaction.

steps.title: Pay partners and cover the running costs
steps.text: Divide payment under the agreed terms and pay delivery, site, staff and technology bills. Fund new services while they build demand.

specifics.title: A new grocery site needs enough orders
specifics.text: Rent, staff and handling costs begin before a site is busy. An established location with repeat customers may perform differently from one that has just opened. Count useful demand as well as site openings.

specifics.title: Membership benefits have a cost
specifics.text: A subscription can encourage people to return or try another service. Discounts and delivery benefits still have to be paid for; selling a membership does not show that every order placed with it makes money.

specifics.title: The set of businesses can change
specifics.text: The company can start trials, change services or sell an activity. Use the period’s business notes and later announcements rather than assuming every older feature or acquired business remains in the group indefinitely.

watch: Are more people returning and placing orders?
Demand supported by repeat use can differ from demand bought through discounts.

Read paying-user activity, order frequency and the amounts ordered alongside promotions. Keep meal, grocery and dining activity separate, and do not substitute total registered accounts for actual purchasing customers.
Are Instamart locations becoming busy enough to support their costs?
More locations can increase spending before they improve earnings.

Compare older and newer sites where the company provides that information. Read rent, picking, delivery and availability with order activity, and check which costs any quoted profit measure leaves out.
What remains from each business after its own costs?
Selling goods and charging service fees are different ways of earning money.

Read the reported meal-delivery, dining, grocery, distribution and newer-service results separately. Keep losses visible and remove sales between group businesses when comparing with the group’s final revenue.
Do restaurants, sellers and delivery partners keep providing a useful service?
Customers return when selection, availability and delivery work well.
Read partner availability, delivery quality and changes in terms or operating rules. Higher fees may raise income but can also change what restaurants, sellers and customers choose to do.
Can growth be funded without confusing profit with cash?
New sites and service trials can need money before they pay their way.

Read cash from running the business, equipment spending and future rental commitments. Follow the adjustments from headline earnings to final profit, and check business sales or closures before assuming old revenue will repeat.
risks: Discounts and advertising can prevent rising demand from producing enough earnings.
Late, missing or unavailable items can weaken repeat use and create extra costs.
New sites and experiments keep losing money
Expansion can require continued funding while demand develops.
Food safety, consumer rights, worker arrangements, data protection or partner disputes can affect costs and service.
context: Storage and delivery are real jobs behind an online order

The group’s business services can help merchants hold and move goods before a household ever places an order. Read what customers are paying for in each activity rather than treating the entire company as only a restaurant-delivery app.
quiz: If restaurant delivery earns a profit, must the whole Swiggy group be profitable?
No. Grocery delivery, newer services and company-wide expenses can use more money than another activity earns. Read all the business results and the costs still left to deduct.
sources: FY26 shareholder letter and segment definitions

financialNotes.title: The existing table uses the financial statement’s measure
financialNotes.text: It preserves external revenue after inter-segment adjustments and the reported segment result. Adjusted EBITDA and gross order value must not be substituted into those columns.

financialNotes.title: Read the losses as part of the business story
financialNotes.text: The verified snapshot shows different outcomes across food delivery, out-of-home, quick commerce, supply chain and innovations. Segment results still require the source’s reconciliation for other income, share-based payments, finance, depreciation and other items before group net profit.
